title: Around the World, Arm to Arm
summary: After Jenner's book, vaccination spread around the world amazingly fast. To carry the living vaccine across the ocean, a Spanish doctor and a nurse named Isabel Zendal sailed with 22 orphan boys, passing the cowpox from one boy's arm to the next like a relay race. Not everyone liked vaccines, though, and cartoonists even joked that people would sprout cows!

sections.heading: News Travels Faster Than Ships
paragraphs: In 1798, Edward Jenner's little book about cowpox was printed in England. Within a few years, it had been translated into many European languages, and doctors from Spain to Russia were reading it and trying vaccination for themselves. For a world with no telephones, no internet and no trains, that was astonishingly quick.

Why did it spread so fast? Partly because smallpox was everywhere and everyone feared it, so a safer way to beat it was huge news. Partly because Jenner and his supporters were generous: Jenner sent samples of vaccine to almost anyone who asked, usually for free, and did not try to keep the method secret or make money from selling it. And partly because the method was simple. You did not need a laboratory, only a lancet, a steady hand and some fresh cowpox material.

Vaccine crossed the Atlantic quickly too. In 1798 a doctor named John Clinch began vaccinating in Trinity, Newfoundland, which was then a British colony. In New York in 1799, the physician Valentine Seaman vaccinated his own children. In Boston, Benjamin Waterhouse, a professor at Harvard's medical school, obtained vaccine from England and in 1800 vaccinated four of his own children. He is often credited with the first vaccinations in the United States, though as you can see, Seaman had already started in New York, and several doctors were working at almost the same time.

Waterhouse wanted powerful supporters, so he wrote to Thomas Jefferson, who was soon to become President of the United States. Jefferson, who loved science, answered in December 1800 and quickly became one of vaccination's most enthusiastic champions. He had members of his household and many people at his home, Monticello, in Virginia, vaccinated, and he helped Waterhouse spread the vaccine to doctors in the South.

On 14 May 1806, exactly ten years after James Phipps was vaccinated, Jefferson wrote a famous letter to Jenner. He thanked him on behalf of humanity, and predicted that one day, thanks to Jenner, people in the future would only know from history books that the terrible disease of smallpox had ever existed. It was a bold prediction. It would take more than 170 years to come true, but it did.

Even enemies agreed on vaccination. Britain and France were at war for most of the years between 1793 and 1815, yet Napoleon had his soldiers vaccinated, and he awarded Jenner a medal. Across the continent, governments began to set up vaccination programmes. Doctors, priests and local officials encouraged parents to bring their children. Vaccination had become one of the first truly international medical ideas.

sections.heading: A Living Relay: Arm to Arm
paragraphs: There was a catch. The vaccine was a living virus, though nobody yet knew what a virus really was. It had to be fresh to work. Today vaccines are made in factories and kept cold in fridges, but in 1800 the only reliable place to keep cowpox alive was inside a living body, either a cow's or a person's.

Remember from the last part that Jenner discovered cowpox could be passed from person to person. That made a clever system possible, called arm-to-arm vaccination. It worked like a relay race. A child was vaccinated. About a week later, a small blister had formed on their arm, filled with clear fluid that people called lymph. A doctor would gently prick the blister with a lancet and use that fresh fluid to vaccinate the next child. A week after that, the second child's blister could be used for a third child, and so on. As long as the chain was not broken, one cow's cowpox could be kept going for years and passed to thousands of people.

Doctors also tried to send vaccine by post or by ship. They dried the lymph on threads, on the tips of quills or between little pieces of glass, then sealed them up. Sometimes this worked over short journeys in cool weather. But on long voyages, especially through hot climates, the dried vaccine often died before it arrived, and when a doctor at the other end tried to use it, nothing happened. Over and over, attempts to send vaccine to faraway places simply failed.

Arm-to-arm vaccination had its own dangers. If a child in the chain carried another infection in their blood, the lancet could carry it along with the cowpox. Over the 1800s, doctors realised that occasionally diseases such as syphilis, a serious infection that was hard to detect, and skin infections such as erysipelas had been passed on this way. One modern estimate suggests syphilis was spread in roughly 750 out of every 100 million arm-to-arm vaccinations. That is a very small fraction, but with millions of vaccinations a year, it was a real problem and a real cause of fear. It became one of the strongest reasons people looked for a better way to make vaccine.

Still, for most of the 1800s, arm-to-arm vaccination was how the world was protected. Parents in many towns were asked to bring their child back eight days after vaccination so that other children could be vaccinated from their arm. Some families were proud to help. Others hated the idea. Either way, a great river of cowpox flowed from arm to arm through the century, linking millions of people who never met.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two Boys and a Ship Called María Pita
paragraphs: Now imagine the problem facing the King of Spain. In the early 1800s, Spain ruled a huge empire stretching across much of the Americas, from what is now the southern United States down through Mexico, Central America and much of South America, and across the Pacific to the Philippines. Smallpox killed huge numbers of people there, especially Indigenous communities. King Charles IV had seen smallpox up close: one of his daughters had been sick with it. He wanted the new vaccine taken to every part of his empire. But how could a living vaccine survive a voyage across the Atlantic Ocean, which took many weeks?

The answer came from a doctor named Francisco Javier de Balmis. He was born in Alicante, Spain, in 1753, the son of a barber-surgeon, and he trained as a military surgeon. He had already served in the Americas and knew Mexico well. He had become one of the King's physicians and had translated a French book about vaccination into Spanish. Balmis came up with a plan that sounds startling today: he would bring the vaccine across the ocean alive, inside a chain of children.

On 30 November 1803, a small ship called the María Pita sailed out of the port of A Coruña, in Galicia in north-west Spain. On board were about 37 people, including doctors, nurses and helpers, and 22 orphan boys, aged roughly 3 to 10, from local orphanages. The plan was to vaccinate two boys at a time. About a week or so later, when the blisters on their arms were ready, material from those blisters would be used to vaccinate the next two boys, and so on, all the way across the sea. Two at a time was a safety measure: if one boy's vaccination did not take, there was a backup.

The ship also carried medical instruments, glass containers for the vaccine, and copies of the vaccination book Balmis had translated, ready to hand out so that local doctors could carry on the work after the expedition left. The official name of the voyage was the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition. Some historians call it the first international public health expedition in history.

The boys could not be left to look after themselves on a crowded sailing ship, and they needed someone to comfort them, keep them clean and keep the different groups apart so the chain would not get mixed up. That job went to a woman named Isabel Zendal. She was the rectoress, or head, of the orphanage in A Coruña where many of the boys had lived, and she brought her own son, Benito, about nine years old, who was one of the children carrying the vaccine. We will come back to her later in this part.

sections.heading: From the Caribbean to China
paragraphs: The María Pita's first stop was Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, where the team spent about a month vaccinating people before sailing on in early January 1804. The Atlantic crossing was the hardest test of the chain. Every week or so, two more boys were vaccinated from the arms of the last two. If the timing slipped, or if both new vaccinations failed, the vaccine would die in the middle of the ocean. It did not. On 9 February 1804, the ship reached Puerto Rico with the vaccine still alive.

There was a small surprise waiting. Vaccine had already reached Puerto Rico from the nearby Danish island of Saint Thomas, so the islanders had begun vaccinating before Balmis arrived. The expedition sailed on to Venezuela, reaching Puerto Cabello on 20 March 1804. In Caracas, Balmis helped set up a vaccination board, a local committee whose job was to keep the vaccine chain going and organise vaccination after the expedition left. It is described as the first such board on the American continent.

At the port of La Guaira, the expedition split in two. Balmis's deputy, a young surgeon named José Salvany, took one group south into what is now Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Chile and Bolivia. His journey through mountains, rivers and jungles lasted about seven years. He became ill and exhausted, and he died in Cochabamba, in today's Bolivia, in 1810, still working. Balmis took the other group north. They reached Havana, in Cuba, on 26 May 1804, and then went on to Mexico, which was then called New Spain. Cuba also sent three enslaved girls to Campeche, in Mexico, to carry the vaccine there in their arms, a reminder that the people whose bodies carried this vaccine often had no choice.

In Mexico, Balmis persuaded the Viceroy, José de Iturrigaray, to have his own son vaccinated, which encouraged many families to follow. Vaccine was carried to many parts of New Spain. Then Balmis set out on an even longer journey. The Pacific Ocean is far wider than the Atlantic, so he needed a new chain of carriers. Twenty-six Mexican children were gathered for the job. On 8 February 1805, they sailed from Acapulco on a galleon, a big trading ship, called the Magallanes. They arrived in Manila, in the Philippines, on 15 April 1805, with the vaccine alive again. There, the Governor-General, Rafael María de Aguilar, set an example by having his five children vaccinated.

Balmis still was not finished. In September 1805 he sailed from Manila to Macau, on the coast of China, and from October he vaccinated people in several Chinese cities as far as the Canton region. On his way home to Spain in 1806 he stopped at the island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, which belonged to Britain. Spain and Britain were at war, but he persuaded the British authorities there to let him vaccinate the islanders. He reached Lisbon, in Portugal, on 14 August 1806, having travelled around the whole world.

Nobody knows exactly how many people were vaccinated by the expedition and the local doctors and boards it trained. Estimates run to hundreds of thousands, and one Spanish account suggests more than half a million. When Jenner heard about the voyage, he wrote that he did not imagine the annals of history furnish an example of philanthropy so noble, so extensive as this.

Isabel Zendal did not go back to Spain. She stayed in Puebla, Mexico, with her son Benito, and the Galician boys never returned home to Galicia. One boy is known to have died during the voyage. For a long time Isabel was almost forgotten. Her name was even spelled in about 300 different ways in old documents. Today she is honoured: in 1950 the World Health Organization recognised her as the first nurse in history to take part in an international health mission, a statue of her stands in A Coruña, and an emergency hospital built in Madrid during the COVID-19 pandemic was named after her.

sections.heading: Calves, Glycerin and a Cleaner Vaccine
paragraphs: The arm-to-arm system was clever, but it had those worrying problems: the chain could break, and occasionally it carried other diseases. In the 1800s doctors began to try a different idea. Instead of keeping the vaccine going in children, why not keep it going in cows, where it had come from in the first place?

From about the 1840s, doctors in parts of Europe, particularly Italy, began to grow vaccine on the skin of young cattle. Here is how it worked. A healthy calf was chosen, and an area of skin on its belly or side was shaved and cleaned. The vaccinator made many small scratches in the skin and rubbed vaccine into them. After several days, the scratches formed rows of blisters, full of vaccine virus. The material from these blisters, called calf lymph, was carefully scraped off and collected. A single calf could provide enough vaccine for a very large number of people. The calf was usually checked afterwards to make sure it had been healthy.

Calf lymph slowly spread, and by the 1880s it had become the leading kind of smallpox vaccine. It had a big advantage: no human blood was involved, so diseases like syphilis could not be passed from one child to another through it. Vaccine farms, sometimes called vaccine stations or institutes, appeared in many countries, with stables of calves kept specially for the purpose.

There was still the problem of bacteria. Material scraped from a calf's skin was not clean, and in 1900 a survey found thousands of bacteria per gram in some vaccine, and far more in some commercial products. An English government scientist named Sydney Arthur Monckton Copeman found an answer. He showed that mixing the vaccine with glycerin, a thick, sweet, colourless liquid, at about half and half, killed off most of the unwanted bacteria while leaving the vaccine still able to work. From 1899, the British government's vaccine establishment gave out only glycerinated calf lymph to public vaccinators.

Glycerinated vaccine still had a weakness. At warm temperatures it lost its strength quickly, which made it hard to use in tropical countries without ice. That problem would not really be solved until the middle of the 20th century, when scientists learned to freeze-dry vaccine into a stable powder, a story you will meet when the world sets out to wipe out smallpox completely.

sections.heading: Sprouting Cows: Fear, Laws and Protests
paragraphs: Not everybody welcomed vaccination. Some people felt it was wrong to put material from an animal into a human body. Some had religious objections; even in the 1720s a preacher had called variolation a 'diabolical operation', and similar arguments were now aimed at vaccination. Others simply did not trust doctors, or had heard frightening rumours. One doctor, William Rowley, published pictures claiming to show children whose faces had become cow-like after vaccination.

In 1802 the brilliant British cartoonist James Gillray turned these fears into a famous joke. His print 'The Cow-Pock, or the Wonderful Effects of the New Inoculation!' shows a crowded room in which a doctor, usually taken to be Jenner, is vaccinating a frightened woman, while all around patients are sprouting little cows from their arms, noses, cheeks and ears. Gillray's prints were displayed in the window of his publisher Hannah Humphrey's shop in London, where crowds gathered to look. Historians argue about whether Gillray was mocking vaccination or mocking the people who were scared of it. Either way, the picture shows how strange and unsettling the new idea seemed to many people.

As governments became convinced vaccination worked, they began to make laws about it. In Britain, the Vaccination Act of 1840 offered free vaccination to the poor and made variolation illegal, because variolated people could spread smallpox. Then, in 1853, a new Act made vaccination compulsory for babies in England and Wales: parents had to have their child vaccinated within three months of birth, or four months for orphans, and could be fined £1 if they did not. Later laws in 1867 and 1871 made the rules stricter, created vaccination officers to enforce them and allowed repeated fines.

Many people were angry. Some objected to the government telling parents what to do with their children's bodies. Some were worried about the real risks of arm-to-arm vaccination. Working-class families, who were most often fined, felt that the law fell hardest on them. In 1854 a writer named John Gibbs published one of the first pamphlets against compulsory vaccination, and in 1867 the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League was formed. Similar groups later appeared in the United States.

The city of Leicester, in the English Midlands, became the centre of the protest. By 1885, more than 3,000 prosecutions of parents were reported to be waiting to be heard there. In 1885 a huge demonstration filled the streets of Leicester. Estimates of how many people took part vary widely: some sources say more than 20,000, while others claim as many as 100,000. The protesters wanted the compulsory laws changed.

The government set up a Royal Commission, a group of experts, to study the whole question; it met from 1889 to 1896. Its advice led to the Vaccination Act of 1898. This kept vaccination compulsory but added a 'conscience clause': parents who sincerely believed vaccination would harm their child could apply for an exemption certificate. People who used it were called conscientious objectors, one of the earliest uses of that phrase. The same law switched government vaccine from human arm-to-arm lymph to calf lymph. In 1907 the rules were relaxed further, so that parents only had to sign a simple declaration. In the United States, a famous 1905 Supreme Court case, Jacobson v. Massachusetts, decided that states could require smallpox vaccination during an outbreak. Debates about how to balance personal choice and protecting the community have continued ever since, and you will meet them again later in this story.

sections.heading: The Mystery of Vaccinia
paragraphs: Here is a twist that would have amazed Jenner. You might expect that the smallpox vaccine used in the 20th century, the one that eventually wiped smallpox off the planet, was simply cowpox. It was not. The modern smallpox vaccine contains a virus called vaccinia, named from the same Latin word for cow. Vaccinia is a close relative of cowpox, but it is not the same virus.

Scientists first showed the difference in 1939, when the British researcher Allan Watt Downie found that vaccinia and cowpox reacted differently in laboratory tests. They were related but distinct. So where did vaccinia come from? Nobody knows for certain. During the 1800s, vaccine was passed through so many arms, calves and laboratories, and records were so patchy, that somewhere along the way the virus being used changed. The CDC, the US public health agency, simply says that at some point in the 1800s the virus used for vaccination switched from cowpox to vaccinia.

Modern genetic studies have given an intriguing clue. When scientists read the full genetic code of vaccinia, they found it is most closely related not to the cowpox found in Britain, but to horsepox, a similar disease of horses. Horsepox seems to have vanished from the wild; the only known sample was collected in Mongolia in 1976. Then researchers studied old vaccine samples kept from the past. A smallpox vaccine made in 1902 by the American company Mulford turned out to be about 99.7 percent similar to horsepox.

Remember that Jenner had suggested cowpox started in horses, carried to cows on the hands of farm workers? Most experts dismissed that idea. It now seems that horses may have been part of the story after all, at least for some of the vaccine strains used in the 1800s and later. Some vaccine makers are known to have used material from horses as well as cows. The most common view today is that vaccinia, cowpox, horsepox and smallpox all share a common ancestor, and that vaccinia's exact origin may never be fully solved.

What mattered most for people in the 1800s was that vaccination worked. Smallpox deaths fell sharply in places where most people were vaccinated, and countries such as Sweden saw what happened when vaccination dropped: in Stockholm, where fewer than half of people were vaccinated in the early 1870s, a major smallpox epidemic broke out in 1873. Yet for all this success, there was something deeply strange about the whole business. Nobody knew why vaccination worked. Nobody knew what cowpox actually was, or what caused smallpox, or any other disease. Many doctors still believed illness came from bad air. The answer would come from microscopes, laboratories and a new idea about invisible living enemies.

deepDive: The Balmis Expedition was, in effect, a living cold chain. A cowpox vaccination produces a blister whose fluid is most useful for passing on at around the end of the first week, so a chain of carriers needs a new person roughly every week to ten days. With 22 boys, vaccinated two at a time, the María Pita could in theory sustain the chain for around ten or eleven links, enough to cover a crossing that took a little over two months from A Coruña to Puerto Rico, including the stay in Tenerife. The double pairing gave redundancy: if one vaccination failed to take, the other still carried the virus. The same logic required 26 new child carriers for the much longer Pacific crossing from Acapulco to Manila. Modern historians praise the scale and ambition of the expedition, which set up local vaccination boards that kept vaccinating long after the ships left, but they also stress its ethical problems: orphans and enslaved girls had no real choice about being used as living containers, and few records tell us what they experienced. Arm-to-arm vaccination raised other issues. Its occasional spread of syphilis, estimated at about 750 cases per 100 million vaccinations, became a major argument of nineteenth-century critics. The shift to calf lymph from the 1840s onward, becoming dominant by the 1880s, and Copeman's discovery that 50 percent glycerin suppressed contaminating bacteria, are early examples of improving vaccine safety by changing manufacturing rather than abandoning a useful tool. The compulsion debate also has lasting importance. Britain's 1853 Act made infant vaccination compulsory, the Leicester protest of 1885 showed the strength of opposition, and the 1898 conscience clause created an early legal model for exemption. In the United States, Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) upheld a state's power to require vaccination, stating that liberty does not mean freedom from restraint at all times and in all circumstances. Finally, genomic research has turned vaccinia into a historical puzzle. Sequencing shows modern vaccinia strains cluster with horsepox, and a 1902 Mulford vaccine is about 99.7 percent identical to horsepox, suggesting that horse-derived material entered vaccine stocks at some point. Because vaccine strains were passaged through humans, cows, horses and laboratories for over a century with poor record-keeping, the precise route may never be known.
funFact: To carry living smallpox vaccine across the Atlantic in 1803, the Balmis Expedition used 22 orphan boys as a relay, vaccinating two at a time so that the cowpox stayed alive on their arms all the way to the Americas.
